opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think convolutional language models are a really interesting point in the design space, and they're actually quite closely related to the line of work I've been doing on state space models. If you go back to S4, one of the key insights was that a linear state space model can be computed in two equivalent ways: as a recurrence, which gives you efficient autoregressive inference, or as a global convolution, which gives you efficient parallel training. So in some sense, SSMs were one of the first modern "long convolution" models, and a lot of the follow-up work, things like Hyena and other long-convolution architectures, took that convolutional view and asked, what if we parameterize the kernel more directly, or implicitly with a small neural network, instead of going through the state space?

On the efficiency question, convolutions have some nice properties. With FFTs you get roughly N log N scaling in sequence length instead of the quadratic cost of attention, and they parallelize very well during training. So for long-context settings, things like audio, genomics, and long documents, they can be much cheaper than Transformers.

But I think there are two main limitations, and they're part of why my own work moved away from pure convolutions toward selective state space models like Mamba.

The first is inference. A general long convolution doesn't automatically give you a compact recurrent state. If your kernel is as long as the sequence, then at generation time you either have to cache the whole history, which is basically the same problem as the KV cache in attention, or you have to distill the convolution into a recurrence after the fact. The state space parameterization is nice because it guarantees a fixed-size state, so generation is constant time per step.

The second, and I think more fundamental, is expressivity. A convolution is linear time-invariant: it applies the same operation at every position regardless of the content. That turns out to be a real weakness for language. Tasks like selective copying or associative recall, where the model has to decide what to remember or ignore based on the actual tokens, are very hard for time-invariant models. Attention does this naturally because it's data-dependent. That was the core motivation for selectivity in Mamba: make the dynamics depend on the input, which breaks the convolutional equivalence. You can no longer compute it as a convolution, so we needed a hardware-aware parallel scan instead, but you gain a lot of modeling power.

So my overall assessment is that convolutional models were an important stepping stone. They showed you could get subquadratic, highly parallel sequence models that are competitive in many domains, especially continuous signals like audio and DNA, where time invariance is a reasonable inductive bias. For language, though, I think the field has largely moved toward data-dependent recurrent models, whether selective SSMs, linear attention variants with gating, or hybrids that mix these layers with some attention. The convolutional ideas haven't gone away, since short convolutions still appear inside many of these architectures as a useful local mixing component, but as the main mechanism for long-range dependencies in language, I think pure LTI convolutions have been overtaken.

r001.rationale: The response describes whole-history caching as an inference limitation of general long convolutions, but does not frame avoiding that cache as the efficiency problem post-Transformer architectures address.

r002.rationale: It says state-space models can run recurrently and that their parameterization guarantees a fixed-size state for generation.

r003.rationale: It discusses content-insensitivity in time-invariant convolutions, but does not identify limited local context as a language-modeling limitation.

r004.rationale: It describes a linear state-space model as computable by global convolution and calls these modern long-convolution models, with kernels spanning the sequence.

r005.rationale: It explains that convolutions apply the same operation regardless of content, while attention is data-dependent and supports selective behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so convolutional language models are actually a really interesting point in the design space, and I think they've been a bit underappreciated. A lot of my own work, going back to S4 and even the earlier HiPPO stuff, was really about convolutions in disguise. The whole insight behind S4 was that a linear time-invariant state space model is mathematically equivalent to a convolution with a very long, structured kernel. So you get this dual view: you can run it as a recurrence at inference time, which gives you constant memory per step, or you can run it as a convolution during training, which is parallelizable and uses FFTs to get you near-linear complexity in sequence length.

So when people talk about things like Hyena, or the work coming out of Stanford and Together on long convolutions, I see those as very much in the same family. The convolutional view is really the thing that made these models trainable at scale in the first place. And honestly, for a lot of tasks, especially ones with a lot of local or smooth structure, like audio, genomics, time series, convolutions are a very natural inductive bias. They're efficient, they're hardware-friendly if you do them right, and they scale gracefully with length.

Where I think they run into trouble is on language specifically. Language has this property where what you need to attend to is very content-dependent. A convolution, by definition, is time-invariant: the same kernel gets applied everywhere, regardless of what the tokens are. So you can get pretty far, you can get surprisingly close to Transformers in perplexity, but you tend to see gaps on things like in-context learning, associative recall, copying, these tasks where the model needs to selectively pull information based on what it's looking at. And that's not an engineering problem, it's a modeling limitation of time invariance.

That's really the motivation for the direction I've been pushing with Mamba and selective state spaces. The idea is to keep the efficiency story, linear-time, no quadratic attention, constant-size state at inference, but make the dynamics depend on the input. And the moment you do that, you lose the convolutional formulation, because the system is no longer time-invariant. So you have to find a different way to make it parallelizable, which is where the hardware-aware scan comes in.

So my honest assessment is: convolutional language models were a necessary and important step. They proved you could get long-context efficiency without attention, and they gave us a lot of the mathematical tools we're still using. But I think of them as a stepping stone rather than the endpoint. The efficiency problem isn't just about complexity in sequence length; it's about doing selective, content-aware computation with a bounded state. And pure convolutions, at least in their standard form, can't do that. Going forward I expect the most interesting work to be in hybrids and in these selective recurrent models, with convolutions playing a supporting role rather than being the whole architecture.

r001.rationale: It contrasts recurrence's constant memory per step and bounded state with attention's quadratic cost, communicating that the model need not retain its full history.

r002.rationale: It mentions recurrence and a constant-size state, but does not clearly explain that the state is a compressed representation of the model's history.

r003.rationale: It discusses content dependence and time invariance as limitations, but does not identify ordinary convolutions' local context as a language-modeling limitation.

r004.rationale: It refers to very long structured kernels and long convolutions, but does not say that global convolutions extend context across the entire preceding sequence.

r005.rationale: It says convolutions apply the same kernel regardless of token content and therefore struggle to pull information selectively, but does not clearly state that attention can choose which past tokens to attend to at each step.

astra-6.text:
I think convolutions are a natural approach to that problem. With attention, every token can interact with every other token, and that becomes expensive as the sequence gets longer. A convolution gives you a more structured way to mix information across the sequence, which can be much cheaper to compute.

The challenge is deciding what structure you can impose without losing the capabilities you care about. A standard convolution uses the same filter regardless of the input. Attention, on the other hand, can look at the content and decide which information is relevant. So making a convolution very long gives you access to more context, but it doesn’t necessarily give you the ability to pick out the right thing from that context.

There’s also a distinction between training and generation. You can compute long convolutions efficiently in parallel during training. But for autoregressive generation, you want to update a small state each time a new token arrives. Some convolutional models, including those built from linear state space models, have an equivalent recurrent representation that lets you do that efficiently. An arbitrary long convolution doesn’t necessarily have that property.

So I see convolutions as a useful building block. The interesting question is how you combine that efficiency with mechanisms that can select information based on the input, and whether the resulting model works well both when you process a whole sequence and when you generate one token at a time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses attention’s cost on long sequences and small-state generation, but does not frame the efficiency problem as avoiding caching everything the model has seen.

r002.rationale: It says some convolutional models have an equivalent recurrent representation that updates a small state as each token arrives, communicating a compressed representation of history.

r003.rationale: It does not identify ordinary convolutions’ local context as a limitation.

r004.rationale: It says a very long convolution provides more context, but does not say global convolutions cover the entire preceding sequence.

r005.rationale: It contrasts a standard convolution’s input-independent filter with attention’s ability to select relevant information based on content.

sol-6.1.text:
I think convolutions are a very natural approach to that problem. One of the expensive things about attention is that it explicitly compares every pair of tokens, so the cost grows quadratically with sequence length. A convolution gives you a different way to mix information across a sequence, and you can compute it very efficiently.

The challenge is that a standard convolution has a fixed window. If you want to model dependencies across a long document, you either have to stack a lot of layers or make that window much larger. And then you have to ask how to parameterize that long convolution so that it actually learns useful structure.

That’s one of the connections to state space models that I find exciting. You can view a linear state space model as a particular way of constructing a very long convolution. During training, you can compute that convolution in parallel, and during generation, you can use the equivalent recurrent representation and maintain a fixed-size state.

So I think there’s a compelling efficiency story there. But efficiency alone isn’t enough. Attention has this very useful ability to look back and select information based on the current input. A fixed convolution doesn’t do that directly. The interesting question is how to get that kind of input-dependent behavior while preserving the computational advantages.

r001.rationale: The response frames the efficiency issue as attention’s quadratic cost, not as avoiding a cache of everything the model has seen.

r002.rationale: It says the recurrent representation maintains a fixed-size state during generation, conveying that history is represented compactly.

r003.rationale: It identifies a standard convolution’s fixed window as a challenge for modeling dependencies across a long document.

r004.rationale: It mentions a very long convolution and long-document dependencies, but does not clearly say the convolution covers the entire preceding sequence.

r005.rationale: It contrasts attention’s ability to select information based on the current input with a fixed convolution’s lack of that direct selectivity.
